scenes.heading: Comparing data sets
scenes.say: Two basketball players both average fifteen points a game. Are they the same kind of player? Not even close. Let's find out how to compare two whole sets of data properly.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Pick the bus you can rely on, not just the one that is fast on average
scenes.science: Compare centre (typical value) AND spread (how much it varies)
scenes.breaks: A bigger spread is not always worse. It just means the values are less consistent.
scenes.say: Imagine two buses. One is usually fast but sometimes forty minutes late. The other is a little slower but always on time. For an exam, you would pick the reliable one. Comparing data is the same: you need the typical value, and how much it varies.

scenes.heading: Same centre, different spread
scenes.say: Here are parallel dot plots on one shared scale. First Mia's dots, bunched around fifteen. Then Zara's, spread from six to twenty-four. Both have a mean and median of fifteen, but Mia's range is four and Zara's is eighteen. Mia is far more consistent.

scenes.heading: An outlier drags the mean
scenes.say: Now waiting times at two cafés. Café A has one awful wait of twenty-six minutes. That outlier drags its mean up to eight, so the mean says Café B is quicker. But the medians are four and a half and seven, so on a typical day Café A is quicker.
scenes.caption: Now waiting times at two cafés. Café A has one awful wait of 26 minutes. That outlier drags its mean up to 8, so the mean says Café B is quicker. But the medians are 4.5 and 7, so on a typical day Café A is quicker.

scenes.heading: Working backwards
scenes.say: Here is a powerful trick. Because the mean is the total divided by the number of values, the total is the mean times the number of values. Rebuild the total first, and missing values become easy.

scenes.heading: Hitting a target mean
scenes.question: Mean of 5 tests is 72. What 6th score makes the mean 75?
scenes.say: Liam averages seventy-two over five tests. His total so far is seventy-two times five, three hundred and sixty. For a mean of seventy-five over six tests he needs four hundred and fifty. So the sixth test must be ninety.
scenes.caption: Liam averages 72 over 5 tests. His total so far is 72 × 5 = 360. For a mean of 75 over 6 tests he needs 450. So the 6th test must be 90.

scenes.heading: Watch out
points: Back-to-back plots: left leaves read outwards
Different-sized groups: compare means, not totals
scenes.say: Three traps. On a back-to-back stem and leaf plot, the left leaves get bigger as they move away from the stem. When groups are different sizes, compare means or medians, not totals. And to combine two groups, add their totals, never just average the two means.

Quick recap. Always compare a centre and a spread. Use the same scale for both groups. If there is an outlier, the median is the fairer typical value. And total equals mean times the number of values. Now try the practice questions!
